Addis Ababa needs a confident African diplomacy that joins national ambition to regional prosperity The author (Archive) By Mohamud A. Ahmed – Cagaweyne The most consequential victory in diplomacy often comes before negotiations begin: the power to decide what the argument is about. Egypt has long understood this. When the Nile dispute is presented principally as a question of Egyptian survival, Ethiopia’s development arrives in the conversation already under suspicion. A dam becomes a threat before it becomes a source of electricity. An upstream population’s aspirations become a problem for downstream officials to assess. Ethiopia is left explaining why its future should be permitted to advance. This is a profoundly unequal starting point. Egypt’s dependence on the Nile is real, and any responsible settlement must protect its people against serious harm. But dependence does not confer ownership. Historical advantage cannot become perpetual jurisdiction over another country’s economic choices. The weakness in Cairo’s approach emerges whenever a legitimate demand for security expands into an expectation of control. Prime Minister Dr. Abiy Ahmed’s recent remarks at the 12th Tana High-Level Forum on Security in Africa offered a constructive foundation for challenging that imbalance. Speaking in Bahir Dar, he placed dependable maritime access within Ethiopia’s long-term security and developmental interests. “For a nation of more than 130 million people, access to the sea is existential,” he said, according to the Ethiopian News Agency’s October 24 report. He also affirmed that Ethiopia would pursue its aspirations through dialogue and mutual benefit. That combination deserves support: clarity about the national interest, coupled with a peaceful method for advancing it. The importance of this argument extends beyond ports. It asks whether Ethiopia’s needs will be treated as enduring realities to accommodate or recurring ambitions to contain. Its population needs reliable electricity, competitive industries, dependable trade routes, and the capacity to withstand external disruption. These requirements will survive changes of government. A regional strategy that assumes Ethiopia can indefinitely absorb the costs of inadequate infrastructure and constrained connectivity mistakes postponed development for permanent acquiescence. National security includes the material foundations of ordinary life. A hospital awaiting equipment, a manufacturer facing uncertain delivery costs, and a farmer seeking access to distant markets all depend upon systems that connect Ethiopia to the world. Abiy’s Tana remarks situated maritime access within that larger concern and linked reliable corridors to African trade and economic opportunity. This provides a persuasive direction for diplomacy: Ethiopia can explain how dependable access would benefit coastal partners, producers and communities along transport routes. Egypt’s leadership should recognize the consistency this demands. A country that asks the world to understand its geographical dependence on the Nile should be prepared to understand Ethiopia’s geographical dependence on transit arrangements. The circumstances differ, but the principle is straightforward. Geography creates vulnerabilities that diplomacy must manage fairly. Cairo weakens its moral authority whenever it seeks broad accommodation for Egyptian necessity while approaching Ethiopian necessity chiefly as a strategic inconvenience. The opening of the ninth Cairo Water Week on October 25 demonstrated Egypt’s sustained capacity to present its priorities internationally. President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi defended downstream security while acknowledging other basin countries’ development rights. sis.gov.eg . That acknowledgment matters. Its practical value, however, depends upon whether upstream development is allowed to alter an unequal distribution of benefits. A right that can be exercised only when existing beneficiaries approve its consequences is precariously close to a privilege granted at their discretion. Cairo’s diplomatic strength lies partly in continuity. Political leaders establish the message; technical institutions elaborate it; diplomats repeat it; conferences and media carry it to wider audiences. Ethiopia should study that discipline. It should also challenge the selective reasoning that can accompany it. The repeated invocation of Egyptian vulnerability does not settle how competing needs should be reconciled. Repetition may establish familiarity, but familiarity is no substitute for an equitable argument. The essential arithmetic is modest: Egypt’s security cannot require Ethiopia’s development to approach zero. Any arrangement built upon that assumption would contain the seeds of its own failure. The basin’s political equation has several populations, several economies and several legitimate claims. A settlement that recognizes only one country’s indispensable needs leaves too many variables outside the calculation. Those excluded interests eventually return as mistrust, resistance and renewed dispute. Ethiopia should therefore begin with the human purpose of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Electricity means a functioning clinic, a productive workshop, a student able to study after sunset and an enterprise capable of expanding. These aspirations deserve the same moral seriousness as downstream concerns. Poverty should never become the invisible baseline against which another country’s security is measured. An Ethiopian household’s exclusion from reliable power is also a deprivation, even when it produces fewer international headlines. At Tana, Dr. Abiy appropriately connected the dam’s achievement to the obligation to deliver reliable electricity, industrial growth, and improved livelihoods. www.ena.et That is the standard Ethiopian leadership should accept. National achievement acquires lasting authority through public benefit. A dam’s significance rests in the opportunities it creates, and Ethiopia’s international case becomes stronger when its domestic performance makes those opportunities visible. Yet a sound Ethiopian argument must examine operational risks rather than assume that a legitimate purpose resolves them. Reservoir management, prolonged drought and downstream planning require evidence and workable cooperation. Ethiopia should support useful information exchange, credible technical assessment and practical procedures for managing disagreement. Such measures demonstrate responsible authority. They also make it harder to turn uncertainty into an unlimited argument against Ethiopian development. Egypt bears a corresponding responsibility: it must distinguish demonstrable risks from demands that preserve its preferred position indefinitely. A request for dependable drought safeguards deserves serious negotiation. An expectation that upstream development must leave every downstream advantage untouched deserves challenge. Existing use matters, but treating it as an immovable ceiling on everyone else’s future would freeze inequality into the rules of cooperation. The United Nations Watercourses Convention provides an important reference through its principles of equitable and reasonable utilization, cooperation and prevention of significant harm. Applying those principles requires attention to relevant law, agreements and circumstances; citing them does not decide every operational dispute. Their broader significance is clear, however: shared water governance requires consideration of multiple interests. It cannot responsibly be reduced to unlimited upstream discretion or permanent downstream predominance. Ethiopia’s strongest response would combine legal precision with scientific openness. Rainfall totals, for example, reveal little without examining seasonality, storage, accessibility and infrastructure. Equally, claims about a dam’s regional benefits require scrutiny of operating conditions. The country should publish credible analysis, acknowledge uncertainty and invite serious examination. Evidence gives diplomacy a foundation that rhetorical escalation cannot supply. Ethiopia does not need to exaggerate its rights to establish that they matter. Maritime access requires the same discipline. Article 125 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea recognizes access and transit rights for landlocked states while requiring agreement on their exercise and protecting transit states’ legitimate interests. It provides a framework for cooperation, not an automatic entitlement to another country’s territory or a particular port. www.un.org Ethiopia can pursue commercial agreements, infrastructure partnerships, leases and dependable transit arrangements through consent. The Prime Minister’s emphasis on dialogue offers the appropriate political foundation. This makes categorical resistance to Ethiopia’s lawful maritime aspirations especially shortsighted. A dependable corridor can generate port revenue, infrastructure investment, employment, and larger markets. The commercial logic is additive: greater Ethiopian activity can enlarge opportunities for coastal economies. Governments should negotiate the distribution of those gains, rather than assume that Ethiopia’s improved access necessarily diminishes their sovereignty. Properly designed agreements can protect both sovereignty and commercial reliability. Recent coordination among Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan warrants careful Ethiopian assessment. Such alignment does not, by itself, prove a covert strategy of destabilization. Nevertheless, any approach that treats constraining Ethiopia as a durable source of regional advantage would be a grave miscalculation. An economically frustrated and politically insecure Horn would offer Egypt little dependable reassurance. Pressure that deepens mistrust can make the cooperation Cairo seeks harder to obtain. Egypt should resist the temptation to treat every Ethiopian gain as an Egyptian loss. That assumption turns diplomacy into a room with narrowing walls. It encourages tactical obstruction while neglecting the larger interest in a capable upstream partner able to negotiate, share information, and implement commitments. Ethiopia’s instability would make those tasks more difficult. Predictability depends upon institutions, and institutions require a viable economic and political foundation. Ethiopia must draw the corresponding lesson at home. National cohesion, accountable government, and administrative competence strengthen external influence. Its citizens deserve institutions that convert national projects into public opportunity and diplomatic commitments into reliable performance. Confidence abroad becomes more credible when supported by competence at home. The defense of Ethiopian interests therefore requires investment in domestic legitimacy alongside forceful international advocacy. It also requires intellectual infrastructure. Ethiopia needs hydrologists who can test scenarios, lawyers who can explain competing obligations, economists who can evaluate corridor arrangements, and scholars who can assess regional developments independently. A credible research institution devoted to Nile cooperation and the Horn’s economic security could contribute substantially. Its value would depend upon transparent methods and freedom to publish inconvenient findings. Scholarship loses authority when its conclusions are assigned in advance. Universities, professional associations, civil society organizations and diaspora specialists should help sustain that effort. Ethiopia should engage the strongest Egyptian arguments, identify weaknesses in its own policies and produce proposals that withstand scrutiny. Knowledge must accumulate across changes of personnel. A country should not have to reconstruct its case whenever a neighboring minister delivers a speech. Tana can support this continuity by connecting African expertise with the practical responsibilities of government. The continental argument must be equally confident. Pan-Africanism cannot mean preserving an inherited hierarchy in which some societies retain established benefits while others are asked to postpone transformation. Nor can it disregard Egyptian vulnerability. Egypt belongs within the African community whose future Ethiopia invokes. A credible African settlement would protect downstream lives while recognizing upstream development as a legitimate and necessary part of continental progress. Dr. Abiy’s Tana remarks deserve support because they connect an enduring Ethiopian priority to dialogue and mutual benefit. Their promise now requires patient negotiation, technically credible proposals, and agreements that partners can trust. Ethiopia should build upon that foundation to present a coherent regional vision: electricity that supports production, corridors that sustain commerce, and institutions that make cooperation dependable. Cairo can help shape that future, but it must reconsider an approach that too readily confuses Ethiopian advancement with Egyptian danger. The Nile cannot become a permanent instrument for rationing another nation’s aspirations. Ethiopia, for its part, should defend its interests with the confidence to negotiate and the discipline to make its proposals credible. Egypt’s water security deserves protection. Ethiopia’s development deserves room to advance. A durable settlement must be built around both realities. About the Author Mohamud A. ethiopia.content: Ethiopian Passport Ranks Among World's Lowest, Limiting Travel to 17 Visa-Free Destinations - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopian Passport Ranks Among World's Lowest, Limiting Travel to 17 Visa-Free Destinations Ethiopian Passport Services Ethiopian passport. 26 October 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) By Bruhan Makong Nairobi — Ethiopian passport holders can travel to only 17 countries without a visa, according to figures attributed to the 2026 Global Passport Power Index, highlighting barriers facing Ethiopian citizens seeking international business, education and cultural opportunities. The index places Ethiopia at position 90 globally, alongside countries including Somalia, Yemen, Syria and Afghanistan, according to the report cited by Passport Rank. Ethiopian citizens can access a further 33 destinations through visas on arrival, while only five African Union member states -- Kenya, Benin, The Gambia, Rwanda and Togo -- are listed as allowing them visa-free entry. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The ranking reflects the restrictions Ethiopian travelers face when seeking to cross borders, with advance visa applications, extensive documentation and processing delays potentially complicating international travel. These barriers can affect businesses seeking to attend trade exhibitions, negotiate deals or build partnerships abroad, as well as students and researchers pursuing academic exchanges and other international opportunities. The report attributes the passport's low standing to a combination of economic conditions, security concerns and diplomatic relations. It says foreign governments commonly consider income levels, security risks, and the likelihood of visa overstays when determining entry requirements. Regional instability and security concerns in the Horn of Africa are also cited as factors contributing to strict visa screening for Ethiopian travelers. The report further points to limited reciprocal visa-waiver arrangements as a constraint on mobility. The restrictions can create challenges for Ethiopian companies seeking to expand internationally, particularly where foreign businesspeople can enter Ethiopia through e-visas or visas on arrival while Ethiopian nationals must undergo more demanding visa procedures to visit potential markets. The report says the consequences extend beyond commerce to academic cooperation, cultural exchanges, and international engagement. Read the original article on Capital FM . That's according to the UN migration agency, IOM . Forces from the Somali and Oromia regions in Southern Ethiopia have been fighting for over two decades over boundary demarcations and resources, with recent escalations since last week sparking a new wave of displacement. Amongst those who fled, nearly 11,000 have sought sanctuary within the large compound of the Oriental Mission Church (OMC), a prominent Korean-American Christian organisation based in Los Angeles, which does missionary and humanitarian work in Kenya, said IOM. Community support The remaining 25,600 people are being hosted by communities along the border. IOM is working with the Kenyan government and the UN refugee agency, UNHCR , to collect and manage displacement data, as well as assess humanitarian needs. So far it has identified needs for water and sanitation, shelter and essential household items, food assistance, health support and protection. It also stresses the need to pay special attention to the needs of host communities, who are accommodating most of the displaced, despite already limited resources. Lindberg takes helm at WFP with call to end famine Luke J. Lindberg took office as Executive Director of the UN World Food Programme ( WFP ) on Monday, calling on donors, partners and supporters worldwide to help sustain the agency's life-saving work. "Conflict is driving people into hunger, and extreme weather and maritime choke points exacerbate this reality," Mr. Lindberg said. "We cannot do it alone. Governments, institutions, businesses, and individuals need to stand with us, fund the work, and help get food to people before it's too late. No more famines." Millions in need As many as 266 million people faced acute hunger worldwide last year, with conflict driving the most severe crises. WFP teams currently operate in 83 countries. Mr. Lindberg succeeds Cindy McCain, who led WFP from April 2023 to May 2026, and Carl Skau, who has served as Acting Executive Director since June. He previously served as Under Secretary for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs at the US Department of Agriculture. Somalia takes the lead as UN mission bows out after three decades The UN's political mission in Somalia will close on Saturday , ending more than three decades of UN missions in the country supporting peace, state-building and reconciliation. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) completes its two-year mandate on 31 October. The Security Council has decided not to renew it, at the request of the Somali Government, which wants to take greater ownership of its own peacebuilding and state-building. The mission's work will pass to Somali institutions and to the UN agencies, funds and programmes already operating in the country. Tribute to those who served Secretary-General António Guterres praised the progress made over the decades and thanked those who made it possible, in particular his successive Special Representatives and the mission's staff. He also paid tribute to UN personnel who lost their lives while serving in Somalia. Mr. Guterres acknowledged that Somalia still faces serious political, security, humanitarian and development challenges, and called on the international community to keep up its support so that the gains made are not lost. That means pushing forward with inclusive political dialogue and reconciliation, building stronger institutions, protecting human rights and confronting Al Shabaab, the Somalia-based terrorist group affiliated with al-Qaeda. /UN News Release. somalia.content: Somalia Baidoa Clashes: Federal and Regional Forces Fight | Kulu Media Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Connect with us Search Kulu Media Somali Federal Troops Clash With Regional Forces Near Baidoa Home Latest News Ethiopia Tigray Eritrea Sudan Africa World Politics Economy Finance Business Education More Analysis Entertainment Tech Health Sports English English ትግርኛ አማርኛ Home » News » Africa » Horn of Africa » Somali Federal Troops Clash With Regional Forces Near Baidoa Horn of Africa Somali Federal Troops Clash With Regional Forces Near Baidoa Federal troops and Laftagareen loyalists clash outside Baidoa amid rival claims. Published 45 seconds ago on October 26, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Security personnel patrol a street in Baidoa, Somalia, on September 3, 2026. Renewed clashes were reported outside the city on October 26. (AP Photo/File) Somali federal troops clashed with fighters loyal to former South West State President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen near Baidoa on October 26, 2026, as a continuing dispute over regional control triggered renewed fighting in southern Somalia. The Somalia Baidoa clashes erupted around Burjeedka, on the outskirts of the city, according to AFP reporting . Residents reported explosions, gunfire and military reinforcements moving toward the area. A Somali army commander, Abdullahi Hassan, said government forces had inflicted casualties on their opponents but acknowledged that two soldiers had been killed. A commander loyal to Laftagareen, Hassan Abdulkadir Mohamed, disputed the government’s account, claiming his fighters had forced federal troops to retreat toward Baidoa. Neither side’s claims of battlefield success could be independently verified, and the overall casualty toll remained unknown. Rival Forces Dispute Control of the Battlefield The latest fighting follows weeks of military preparations and territorial changes across South West State. Federal and regional authorities had previously announced plans to recover several towns captured by Laftagareen-aligned fighters. On October 18, Kulu Media documented counteroffensive preparations involving federal and South West State forces. Those preparations focused on strategic locations including Qansaxdheere, Berdale, Buurhakaba, Awdiinle and Diinsoor. The October 26 confrontation near Burjeedka appears to represent another phase of the military struggle surrounding Baidoa, although the precise relationship between the earlier preparations and the latest fighting has not been independently established. Both sides have offered competing accounts of their operations. Witness reports establish that fighting occurred near Baidoa, but the available information does not independently confirm which side controlled the contested positions afterward. Territorial Advances Increased Pressure on Baidoa The latest confrontation follows significant territorial advances by fighters loyal to Laftagareen earlier this month. Between October 8 and 17, his forces reportedly took control of several district centers in the Bay region. Kulu Media previously reported that Laftagareen’s forces seized Diinsoor , along with Berdale, Buurhakaba and Qansaxdheere. The territorial changes brought opposition-aligned fighters closer to Baidoa, the administrative center of South West State. Buurhakaba is particularly important because it lies along the main road connecting Mogadishu and Baidoa, a major transportation corridor for civilian supplies, commercial activity and military movements. Awdiinle, another strategically significant settlement, is located approximately 30 kilometers from Baidoa. The federal government-backed regional administration has rejected the territorial advances and pledged to recover the affected areas. However, the extent of either side’s control over surrounding rural areas remains uncertain. Political Dispute Fuels Repeated Armed Confrontations The conflict stems from a prolonged confrontation between Somalia’s federal government and Laftagareen over political authority in South West State. Federal forces entered Baidoa on March 30, 2026, forcing Laftagareen from the regional capital. Although he subsequently announced his resignation, his supporters continued challenging the legitimacy of the federal government-backed administration. The dispute has repeatedly developed into armed confrontations. On September 3, fighting erupted in Baidoa between federal government forces and militias aligned with Laftagareen. According to the Associated Press, Bay Regional Hospital received 71 wounded people and one dead civilian following those clashes. Somalia’s Defense Ministry accused Laftagareen-aligned fighters of participating in the attack and alleged involvement by Al-Shabaab. Laftagareen’s supporters rejected allegations that they were cooperating with the militant organization. The allegations have not been independently substantiated. The September confrontation also coincided with a reported Doolow drone strike targeting the residence of former Somali commander Mahad Abdirahman Aden, widely known as Mahad Shub. Mahad, a relative and political ally of Laftagareen, survived the attack. The incident generated competing allegations over responsibility, but no independently verified evidence conclusively established who carried out the strike. Together, these developments illustrate how the political confrontation has expanded into a wider security dispute involving military operations, territorial control and competing claims of legitimacy. Civilian Risks Grow Amid Renewed Fighting The renewed violence raises concerns for civilians in and around Baidoa, a major humanitarian center hosting large numbers of people displaced by conflict, drought and food insecurity. Repeated confrontations have disrupted daily life and threatened access to essential services. During the September clashes, residents reported heavy gunfire near populated areas, while medical facilities treated dozens of wounded people. Further fighting around Baidoa could threaten transportation routes used to deliver food, medicine and humanitarian supplies. The latest clashes occurred outside the city, but continued military operations could increase risks for surrounding communities. There was no independently confirmed information on civilian casualties from the October 26 fighting at the time of reporting. Wider Regional and Political Implications The confrontation also comes as Somalia continues its military campaign against Al-Shabaab while facing disagreements over federal authority, constitutional arrangements and elections. Renewed fighting between government forces and rival regional fighters could divert military resources from counterinsurgency operations. The crisis also has implications for neighboring Ethiopia, which maintains troops in Somalia under regional security arrangements. Earlier this month, Ethiopia and Somalia held diplomatic discussions concerning Somali military personnel held in Jigjiga. That separate dispute demonstrates the wider regional security sensitivities surrounding Somalia’s internal military and political developments, although no direct connection to the October 26 Baidoa clashes has been established. For now, the immediate outcome of the fighting near Burjeedka remains disputed. Both federal forces and Laftagareen-aligned fighters have claimed military success, while independent confirmation of territorial control and the full casualty toll remains unavailable. The renewed confrontation underscores the continuing instability in South West State, where political disagreements have developed into repeated armed clashes despite earlier efforts to consolidate federal authority. Published 2 days ago on October 25, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ethiopians who fled fighting in Moyale gather at a holding area in Kenya on October 23, 2026. Photo: Kenya Red Cross Society More than 14,000 Ethiopians have fled deadly fighting in the southern border town of Moyale into neighboring Kenya, as humanitarian agencies warn that shortages of food, clean water and sanitation facilities are threatening thousands of displaced families. The latest figures, reported on Saturday, October 24, 2026, mark a sharp escalation in the Moyale fighting displacement crisis, which began on October 21 amid tensions involving communities from Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional states. According to Anadolu Agency , Kenya Red Cross officials said more than 10,900 displaced people were sheltering in six temporary camps in the Kenyan border town of Moyale, while approximately 4,000 others were staying with relatives and host families. The reported numbers represent a substantial increase from the 2,500 displaced Ethiopians documented in earlier reports on October 23. The growing number of arrivals has intensified pressure on humanitarian services in the Kenyan border region, where emergency responders are struggling to meet the needs of families fleeing the violence. Kenya Red Cross Warns of Critical Shortages The Kenya Red Cross has appealed for additional humanitarian assistance as displaced families face increasingly difficult living conditions. Malik Adan, the organization’s head of the Upper Eastern region, told reporters that emergency shelters urgently needed more food, drinking water, sanitation supplies and toilet facilities. Humanitarian officials warned that inadequate sanitation could increase the risk of diarrheal diseases, particularly in crowded temporary camps where access to clean water and hygiene facilities is limited. The Kenya Red Cross has distributed tents, blankets, sleeping mats and other essential supplies while providing nutritional assistance to children and breastfeeding mothers. Local authorities have also pledged additional food supplies, including rice and beans, but relief workers remain concerned that available resources may be insufficient for the growing displaced population. The latest displacement figures underscore the rapid deterioration of humanitarian conditions since fighting erupted earlier in the week. When the violence first intensified, Kenyan authorities reported that hundreds of Ethiopians had crossed the border, many seeking temporary shelter with relatives and local residents. The movement has since expanded into a much larger humanitarian emergency. Death Toll Feared to Rise as Fighting Continues The humanitarian crisis follows several days of deadly clashes on the Ethiopian side of Moyale. At least nine deaths were reported on October 23, according to hospital information cited in earlier reporting. Humanitarian officials now fear that the overall death toll may have exceeded a dozen, although an updated casualty figure has not been independently confirmed. Residents have reported continued gunfire and shelling in affected areas, raising concerns about further casualties and displacement. The fighting has been linked to tensions between Oromo and Somali communities in southern Ethiopia. According to Anadolu Agency, a dispute involving the display of the Somali Regional State flag in an area administered by Oromia contributed to the latest confrontation. However, the precise sequence of events that triggered the violence, the identities of all armed participants and responsibility for individual attacks remain incompletely verified. The fighting has also affected civilians on the Kenyan side of the border. Earlier reports documented a woman injured by a stray bullet in Kenyan Moyale, demonstrating how violence close to the international boundary can threaten communities in both countries. The town serves as a commercial and transportation link between the two countries, supporting cross-border trade and economic activity. Continued insecurity threatens to disrupt business operations, transportation and the movement of goods, potentially affecting communities whose livelihoods depend on the border economy. The arrival of thousands of displaced Ethiopians has also placed additional pressure on Kenyan host communities. While temporary camps accommodate most of those reported to have crossed the border, thousands are staying with relatives and local families. Such arrangements can provide immediate protection but may become increasingly difficult to sustain if the fighting continues and displaced families are unable to return home. The crisis has also created additional demands on local healthcare facilities, water supplies and emergency services. Humanitarian Response Faces Growing Challenges The rapid rise in displacement highlights the difficulty of responding to sudden population movements in areas where humanitarian resources are already limited. The Kenya Red Cross and local authorities are coordinating relief efforts, but additional assistance may be needed if more civilians cross the border. The emergency is unfolding against a wider backdrop of humanitarian funding challenges in the Horn of Africa. Earlier this month, the United Nations refugee agency warned that funding shortages had disrupted protection services for refugees in Ethiopia, including the suspension of registration affecting tens of thousands of Eritrean and South Sudanese refugees. That separate crisis illustrates broader pressure on humanitarian operations across the region, although it is not directly connected to the Moyale fighting. For families fleeing Moyale, the immediate concerns remain personal safety, temporary shelter, clean water, food and access to medical care. The latest displacement figures suggest that the consequences of the fighting have extended well beyond the original areas of confrontation. Share FILE NATION: United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) will conclude its mandate on October 31, ending a two-year transition and more than three decades of UN missions supporting peacebuilding, governance and state-building in the country, a UN official said Monday. In a statement, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres’ spokesman, Stephane Dujarric, said the mission would cease operations in accordance with Security Council resolutions and a request from Somalia’s federal government. “This milestone brings to a close more than three decades of United Nations missions in support of peacebuilding, state-building, governance and reconciliation in Somalia,” Dujarric said. The closure follows a jointly agreed transition roadmap under which UNTMIS’s mandated responsibilities have been transferred to Somali institutions and UN agencies, funds and programmes. The man had been placed in isolation after health authorities determined that he had direct contact with a person infected with Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease who later died in Kenya. advertisements “Following up on the statement issued on October 12, 2026, the Ministry shares with the Somali public the latest information regarding the Somali citizen who was placed under quarantine,” the Health Ministry said. The ministry said the man was transferred on Oct. 12 to an Ebola quarantine and treatment center at Forlanini Hospital in Mogadishu, where he was monitored under infection-control protocols. He underwent two Ebola tests, one conducted in Somalia and another sent abroad for confirmation. Both returned negative, the ministry said. The man also remained free of Ebola symptoms throughout the quarantine period and completed 21 days of monitoring, the maximum incubation period generally used for Ebola contact follow-up. “Taking into account the results of both tests, the completion of the monitoring period, the citizen’s health status, and an assessment of public health risks ... the Ministry of Health has decided to release the citizen from quarantine,” the statement said. Somalia’s Health Ministry also stressed that no Ebola cases have been confirmed in the country. Health Minister Dr. Ali Haji Adan said authorities would continue surveillance and monitoring as the regional outbreak develops. The exposure was linked to Kenya’s first confirmed case of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease, an imported case involving a man who had traveled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on Oct. 3. He tested positive on Oct. 5 and died later that day, according to the World Health Organization. Kenyan authorities initially identified dozens of contacts connected to the case and placed high-risk contacts under quarantine. By Oct. 20, Kenya had reported nine Bundibugyo Ebola cases, including deaths, all linked to the original imported case, according to WHO. Somali health authorities have not reported any locally acquired or imported confirmed Ebola infection. The figures were shared by the Presidency’s official account , quoting President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, who has repeatedly framed the introduction of one-person, one-vote elections as Somalia’s return to a democratic path abandoned 57 years ago. The president has also claimed that “not a single armed incident occurred at any polling station across the country” and commended politicians who accepted the results despite their disagreements. A Partial Picture The president’s numbers are technically accurate for the districts where voting has taken place, notably in South West State, Galmudug, Hirshabelle, and the Banadir region. In Hirshabelle, the Justice and Solidarity Party secured 78 of 99 parliamentary seats with 114,633 votes cast, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the election results . But the figures describe a process that remains incomplete and deeply contested. The 50 districts covered represent just over half of the 92 districts that existed in 1991. More importantly, the opposition Somali Future Council, which includes the Puntland and Jubaland administrations, has rejected the federal government’s electoral timetable and the constitutional amendments that extended the president’s term. The opposition has not rejected direct elections as a principle. It has rejected the process by which they are being implemented, arguing that major decisions on elections should be reached through dialogue and consensus rather than unilateral action. The Somali Future Council has stated it is ready for “genuine dialogue to reach an electoral agreement and a realistic, implementable timetable,” but has demanded that the president halt what it describes as unilateral measures. The Timing of the Announcement Villa Somalia’s decision to release these figures now, rather than waiting for the National Consultative Forum it has invited the opposition to attend from November 14 to 18, is politically significant. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the invitation , the government has extended a formal invitation to Nabad iyo Nolol, the Somali Future Council, the National Unity Forum, and the Civil Society Coalition to discuss federal election matters. But by presenting the electoral process as a success with concrete numbers before those talks begin, the president is establishing facts on the ground. The implicit argument is that if 1.8 million Somalis have registered and 1,435 officials have been elected, the process has a legitimacy that its opponents cannot deny. Those who reject it are rejecting the will of the people. Critical Note The figures are real, but they are not the whole story. A process can produce real votes and real officials while still being politically contested. The JSP’s victories in Hirshabelle and Galmudug were achieved in elections that the principal opposition parties either boycotted or were excluded from. The Galmudug rerun excluded Towfiiq, the party that had successfully challenged the original vote in court. The Hirshabelle vote proceeded despite the Xawaadle clan’s declaration that it would not accept any election without a prior political agreement. The president’s claim that no armed incidents occurred at polling stations may be technically true in some districts, but it ignores the armed Macawiisley fighters who seized voter registration centres in Beledweyne, the curfews and security restrictions that accompanied the votes, and the broader political violence engulfing South West State, where Laftagareen-aligned forces are fighting federal troops. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the political crisis , Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni has warned that Somali statehood is at risk and called for urgent national dialogue. The real test of the government’s electoral project is not the number of registered voters or elected officials. It is whether the process can produce a result that the opposition and the regional administrations are willing to accept. The November forum is the government’s opportunity to demonstrate that it is serious about consensus. Releasing triumphalist statistics before the talks begin suggests the opposite. It suggests that the government sees the forum not as a negotiation, but as a ratification exercise. If that is the case, the figures will not resolve the crisis. They will deepen it. football.title: الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا - شبكة مصدر الاخبارية
football.content: الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا - شبكة مصدر الاخبارية الرئيسية فلسطينيو 48 شؤون إسرائيلية عربية وإقليمية اقتصاد تكنولوجيا تقارير خاصة رياضة منوعات إتصل بنا الرئيسية رياضة الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا نواذيبو الموريتاني يعوض خسارة الذهاب ويبلغ الدور المقبل.. وقرعة المجموعات تُجرى الأربعاء المقبل الأفريقي التونسي والمغرب الفاسي والهلال السوداني إلى مجموعات دوري أبطال أفريقيا 26 أكتوبر 2026 12:00 ص وكالات - واصل الأفريقي التونسي مشواره في دوري أبطال أفريقيا لكرة القدم، بعدما حجز بطاقة التأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات بفوزه على ضيفه تي بي مازيمبي، بطل الكونغو الديمقراطية، بهدف دون رد، الأحد، في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني للمسابقة. وسجل الكاميروني تاديوس نكينغ هدف المباراة الوحيد في الدقيقة الثانية من الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع للشوط الأول، ليمنح الفريق التونسي انتصاراً ثميناً على أرضه، بعد مواجهة اتسمت بأهمية كبيرة للطرفين. وكانت مباراة الذهاب، التي أُقيمت في مدينة لومومباشي الكونغولية الأسبوع الماضي، قد انتهت بالتعادل 1-1، ليحسم الأفريقي التأهل بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 2-1. وبهذا الإنجاز، أصبح الأفريقي الممثل الثاني للكرة التونسية في مرحلة المجموعات هذا الموسم، إلى جانب غريمه التقليدي الترجي التونسي، فيما تبخرت آمال مازيمبي في مواصلة مشواره نحو اللقب السادس في تاريخه، والأول منذ عام 2015. ويطمح الأفريقي إلى استعادة أمجاده القارية والمنافسة على لقبه الثاني في البطولة، بعدما سبق له التتويج بدوري أبطال أفريقيا عام 1991. نواذيبو الموريتاني يقلب تأخره ويعبر إلى المرحلة الرئيسية وفي العاصمة الموريتانية نواكشوط، انتزع نواذيبو بطاقة التأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات، بعدما تغلب على ضيفه سان بيدرو الإيفواري بنتيجة 2-0، على ملعب «شيخ ولد بيديا»، في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني. وبدأ الفريق الموريتاني المواجهة بقوة، وافتتح كارتييه ديمبيلي التسجيل في الدقيقة العاشرة، ليمنح أصحاب الأرض تقدماً مبكراً أعاد المواجهة إلى نقطة التعادل في مجموع المباراتين. وفي الدقيقة 53، أضاف شيخ خطاب الهدف الثاني لنواذيبو، ليعزز فرص فريقه في حسم بطاقة التأهل ويمنحه الأفضلية اللازمة بعد خسارة مباراة الذهاب بنتيجة 2-1 خارج أرضه. وبهذا الفوز، عوض نواذيبو خسارته في اللقاء الأول، ليتفوق بنتيجة 3-2 في مجموع المباراتين، ويواصل حضوره في المنافسات القارية، بعدما نجح في استثمار عاملي الأرض والجمهور لحسم المواجهة. ويمثل التأهل خطوة مهمة للنادي الموريتاني، الذي نجح في تجاوز عقبة منافس إيفواري بعد مواجهة امتدت حساباتها إلى المباراتين، ليحجز مكانه بين أندية مرحلة المجموعات. المغرب الفاسي يحسم التأهل بهدف قاتل في أبيدجان بدوره، تأهل المغرب الفاسي إلى مرحلة المجموعات، بعدما حقق فوزاً ثميناً على أسيك ميموزا الإيفواري بنتيجة 2-1 في العاصمة أبيدجان، مستفيداً من تعادله في مباراة الذهاب بنتيجة 1-1 في مكناس. وبعد انتهاء الشوط الأول بالتعادل السلبي، افتتح الكونغولي كريستوفر إيبايي التسجيل للمغرب الفاسي، قبل أن يتمكن كيفين باكارا من إدراك التعادل لأسيك ميموزا، لتزداد صعوبة المواجهة مع اقتراب نهايتها. وبينما كانت المباراة تتجه إلى ركلات الترجيح، خطف خالد بابا هدف الفوز للمغرب الفاسي في الدقيقة السابعة من الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع، ليمنح فريقه انتصاراً خارج أرضه بنتيجة 2-1 ويحسم تأهله. وجاء الهدف المتأخر ليضع حداً لمواجهة قوية بين الفريقين، ويمنح النادي المغربي بطاقة العبور بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 3-2. ولحق المغرب الفاسي بمواطنه نهضة بركان، وصيف البطولة، الذي ضمن بدوره التأهل بعد إقصاء ستار سبورت أكاديمي السيراليوني، بالفوز عليه ذهاباً وإياباً. ويعزز تأهل الفريقين الحضور المغربي في المرحلة المقبلة من البطولة، بعدما نجحا في تجاوز منافسيهما في الدور التمهيدي الثاني. الهلال السوداني يكرر فوزه على سيداما بونا وفي العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي، التي يتخذها الهلال السوداني ملعباً بيتياً، كرر الفريق فوزه على ضيفه سيداما بونا الإثيوبي بنتيجة 2-0، ليحجز مقعده في مرحلة المجموعات. وكان الهلال قد فاز بالنتيجة نفسها في مباراة الذهاب، ليحسم التأهل بمجموع المباراتين بنتيجة 4-0، مؤكداً تفوقه على منافسه في المواجهتين. وجاءت ثنائية الفريق السوداني في الشوط الأول، إذ افتتح إرنست لوزولو التسجيل في الدقيقة 33، قبل أن يضيف محمد عبد الرحمن «الغربال» الهدف الثاني في الوقت المحتسب بدلاً من الضائع للشوط. ومنح الانتصار الهلال فرصة مواصلة مشواره القاري، كما عوض جماهيره جزئياً عن خروج غريمه التقليدي المريخ من المسابقة، بعدما ودع البطولة السبت على يد حوريا الغيني بركلات الترجيح. وبهذا التأهل، يواصل الهلال تمثيل الكرة السودانية في البطولة، وسط تطلعات إلى تقديم أداء قوي في مرحلة المجموعات والمنافسة على بلوغ الأدوار الإقصائية. سيمبا وكولوم يكملان قائمة المتأهلين وشهدت بقية مباريات الدور التمهيدي الثاني تأهل سيمبا التنزاني، بعدما حقق فوزاً عريضاً على فريق 15 أوغوستو القادم من غينيا الاستوائية المجموعات من دوري أبطال أفريقيا، المقرر إجراؤها الأربعاء المقبل، حيث ستتحدد مواجهات المرحلة المقبلة ومسارات المنافسة نحو الأدوار الإقصائية. وتكتسب القرعة أهمية كبيرة بالنسبة إلى الفرق التي تجاوزت football.summary: حسم الهلال السوداني تأهله إلى دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بعد فوزه على سيداما كوفي الإثيوبي بهدفين دون رد في إياب الدور التمهيدي الثاني، ليحقق مجموع 4-0 في مباراتي الذهاب والإياب. وقد أظهر الهلال أداءً قويًا خلال المباراتين، مما يعكس استعداده الجيد للمنافسات المقبلة. في المقابل، تمكن المغرب الفاسي من خطف بطاقة التأهل في مباراة مثيرة ضد أسيك ميموزا الإيفواري، حيث انتهت المباراة بفوز المغرب الفاسي 2-1. سجل كريستوفر إيباي هدف التقدم للمغرب الفاسي في الدقيقة 62، لكن أسيك ميموزا أدرك التعادل في الدقيقة 73. ومع ذلك، سجل خالد بابا هدف الانتصار القاتل في الدقيقة 97، ليقود فريقه إلى التأهل بمجموع 3-2. هذه النتائج تعكس تنافسية البطولة وتوقعات مثيرة للجولات القادمة.
